turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the system's crawling. Bear with me a second. Right, what's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): This cough. It's been going on for weeks and I'm absolutely knackered. I just want it dealt with.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): OK. Cough. Are you bringing anything up, or is it dry?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Dry. Nothing comes up. I reckoned it was a cold, that's all.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the cold actually start? I'm just opening your notes, they're taking an age.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't tell you the day. I had a sniffle and a bit of a sore throat, that cleared up, and the cough just stayed. Don't ask me for a date, I haven't got one.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the window froze. Say the cold bit again?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The cold's gone. Sniffles gone. Cough is what's left, a couple of weeks I suppose, maybe, I don't know.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Temperature, sweats?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I checked. No temperature.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain in the chest?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It doesn't hurt.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath at all?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not really. I can still get round the house.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're on blood pressure treatment, aren't you. The medication tab won't load. What are you actually taking?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril. They started it recently. Before that, amlodipine, but I stopped it in March, ankles blew up like balloons.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped the amlodipine in March. And the ramipril dose?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Five milligrams? Or two point five. Packet's at home. I take it in the morning, when I remember.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you remember, meaning you skip some?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The odd morning, yeah. I'm not doing it on purpose. I'm tired, I forget, so don't make a thing of it.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): List's up. Ramipril 5 milligrams once a day, issued three weeks ago. Amlodipine 5 milligrams, recorded as stopped, which fits with March.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks for the tablet, maybe. The cough is longer, five or six weeks. It was already going before my sister's birthday, and I'm not working the date out for you.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five or six weeks, say that again? I was looking at the pressure.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Five or six weeks of this cough. Since you're in the notes, what's the pressure doing?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): 156 over 94. Pulse 78. Not awful, not brilliant either.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Lovely. And I'm not sleeping. It wakes me two or three times a night, then I'm useless all the next day.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Just the cough waking you, or any wheeze with it?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I already said I'm not short of breath. It's the cough. Can we move on? I've been in that waiting room ages.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any phlegm overnight, even a scrap?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bone dry. Tickly, right at the back of the throat.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen. Big breath... and again. Chest is clear, no crackles, no wheeze just now. Throat's a bit red, mind.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Feels scratchy, yeah. My sister takes lisinopril for her blood pressure, she coughed on it and they changed her. I nearly nicked one of hers, but I didn't, before you start.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't take other people's tablets. Lisinopril's the same group as ramipril. You definitely didn't swallow any?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I didn't. I just said.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Anything you have taken for the cough?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Benylin, the chesty cough one from the chemist. One dose, felt sick, so that was the end of that. And some doctor mentioned atorvastatin once, I never started it, so don't bother adding it.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): One dose of Benylin, then stopped. We'll leave the statin, you never took it. Ankles swollen at the moment?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that was the amlodipine, they're fine now. There was another tablet years ago, before the amlodipine, a little white one for the pressure, once a day. I don't know the name. I stopped it ages ago, it didn't suit me.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No name at all for that white one?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. White and small, that's the lot. My head's pounding as well, if anyone cares. This room is boiling.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pounding, an actual headache, or just the waiting?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): An actual headache. Behind the eyes. Not terrible. It's when I haven't slept.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Going back to the breathing, because I want this straight. You were sure there's no shortness of breath.

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, when a bad bout hits I do get puffed. I have to sit on the edge of the bed till it eases. I'm not gasping all day, only with the cough, and I should have said.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only with the cough. And in those moments, chest pain, or still no?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Still no pain. Just the puffing and the hacking.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud, so ignore the muttering. Dry cough, a cold in the background, and a new ACE inhibitor. It might be the ramipril, it might just be the tail of that cold, and I'm not putting a firm label on the cough today.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't know. I came all this way for might. Fantastic.

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know you're fed up. What I will do is stop the ramipril from today. Same family as your sister's lisinopril, and these coughs can hang about. I'll start losartan instead, 50 milligrams once a day, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Losartan. And the cough just vanishes, does it? Do I take the ramipril tonight or not? Speak plainly.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): No more ramipril, starting now. If the cough is the tablet, it can still take a few weeks to fade, so don't expect a miracle overnight. If it hasn't settled, we might arrange a chest x-ray, not today.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): More waiting. Someone's going to want blood tests as well, they always do.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'll put a form in for kidney function and electrolytes, this week, before we leave you on the losartan. Reception can book it.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I'm not traipsing back here every five minutes, though. I'm done in.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in four weeks, so we can check the pressure and whether the cough's easing. If the breathing with the cough gets worse before that, don't sit on it, come sooner or ring the surgery.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Right. Is that it? I want a cup of tea and a lie-down, not another lecture.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nearly. You miss the odd dose, so losartan is every morning, try not to skip it. Paracetamol for the headache if you need it. I never asked about allergies and the clinic's overrunning, so we'll leave that; the form's at reception.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Drug, dose, frequency, duration, indication supported; status wrong because ramipril is stopped later today.
bad.text: ramipril (dose=5 mg, frequency=once a day, duration=3 weeks, indication=high blood pressure, status=currently_used, reported_by=doctor)

omissions.text: Ramipril adherence detail: patient takes it in the morning when remembered and misses the odd morning dose.
Amlodipine was stopped because it caused ankle swelling 'like balloons'.
Patient denied sweats when asked with fever/temperature.
Cough described as 'bone dry' and tickly, right at the back of the throat.
Doctor asked about wheeze overnight; no wheeze symptom was reported by the patient, only cough waking them.
Patient reported nausea/feeling sick after one dose of Benylin, leading to stopping it.
Atorvastatin was mentioned previously but the patient never started it.
Patient definitely did not take any of sister's lisinopril despite considering it.
Plan detail: kidney function and electrolytes blood test is to be done this week, and reception can book it.
Safety-net wording included to come sooner or ring the surgery if breathing with the cough gets worse before the 4-week review.
Allergies were not asked/confirmed; doctor explicitly said 'I never asked about allergies'.

omissions.text: Patient initially denied shortness of breath ('No. Not really. I can still get round the house') before later clarifying they do get puffed only during bad coughing bouts.
Ramipril adherence detail: patient takes it in the morning and misses the odd morning dose because they forget.
Amlodipine was stopped in March because it caused ankle swelling; timing in March was stated by the patient and confirmed by the doctor.
Patient said they had considered taking their sister's lisinopril but definitely did not take any.
Atorvastatin was mentioned previously but the patient never started it, so it should not be added as a current/past taken medication.
Cough is disturbing sleep and leaves the patient 'useless all the next day' due to poor sleep.
Examination finding was 'no crackles, no wheeze just now'—the absence of wheeze was specifically qualified as at the time of examination.
Allergies were not asked/recorded during the consultation; doctor explicitly said they had not asked about allergies and would leave it because clinic was overrunning.
